newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: China talk puts European feeds on firm footing.
newsitem.headline: China talk puts European feeds on firm footing.

text.p: Rumours of Chinese soybean buying lifted the Chicago-traded futures on Friday and put the European meals and feeds market on a firm footing on Monday, where many traders are still keeping a wary eye on the weather.

Chicago Board of Trade soybean futures jumped on Friday amid market talk that China had purchased up to three cargoes of U.S. soybeans for May/June delivery, pushing the May contract up 20-3/4 to $8.67-3/4 a bushel.
In Europe, physical traders were offering South American soymeal up to $10 a tonne higher. There were no early trades.
Far East traders could not confirm the Chinese deals but said they were possible, despite U.S. beans being more expensive than South American material.
European traders said they also had no confirmation but one -- citing usually reliable U.S. sources -- reckoned the deal involved one cargo of U.S. beans and two from Brazil.
"But this is still hearsay with nothing definite," he said.

Chicago traders said the tight U.S. carryout also made the deal unlikely. In its April forecast the U.S. Agriculture Department said only 125 million bushels of soybeans would be on hand at the end of August, the lowest stocks total for 20 years.
European traders added there was now market speculation that next month's forecast would show a further decline in stocks, down to as low as 105 million bushels.
An additional break on business on Monday was the firm dollar, which was quoted up above 1.73 marks in early trade.

The weekend's badly needed rain in northwest Europe and France over the weekend could dispell some of the fears over grain crops being damaged by drought but traders said a potential crisis had yet to be diverted.

A dry spell in much of northwest Europe has helped drive world wheat prices to 1997 highs around $4.25 per bushel in Chicago futures. The European Union imposed a tax on Thursday to curb wheat exports and thereby keep a lid on internal prices.
"The question is now whether the rain that fell is sufficient," one trader said.
In France, dry weather was expected to set in again from mid-week.

On top of weather worries, the continuing problem of swine fever could have an impact on the main ingredients for pigfeed -- tapioca, sunflowerseedmeal and rapemeal. Analysts estimate the government's cull of around one million pigs so far would cut demand for pigfeed by between five and ten percent by the end of the year.

But this will be a tough week to do business in any great volume as traders in the Netherlands will be absent on Wednesday, when it is the Queen's Birthday and many other countries will be away on Thursday for May Day celebrations.
